tools.description:

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

content.text:
Claude Code has a few **permission modes** that control how much I can do without asking you. Press **Shift+Tab** to cycle through them. The current mode is shown at the bottom of the prompt.

### Permission modes

| Mode | What it does | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Default** | I ask before editing files or running shell commands, unless you've already allowed that action. Reading and searching don't need approval. | Unfamiliar code, or when you want to review each step |
| **Accept edits** | File edits are approved automatically. Shell commands and other riskier actions still ask first. | You trust the direction and don't want to approve every edit |
| **Plan mode** | Read-only. I can explore the code and write a plan, but I can't edit files or run commands that change anything. When the plan is ready, you approve it before I start. | Large or unclear tasks where you want to agree on the approach first |
| **Auto mode** | A separate classifier model checks each action before it runs. Routine, low-risk actions go through without a prompt. Risky ones get blocked or sent to you, such as deleting things, force-pushing, sending data outside your machine, or going beyond what you asked for. | Longer tasks where you want fewer interruptions but still want guardrails |
| **Bypass permissions** (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`) | No checks at all. Everything runs. | Only in throwaway sandboxes or containers |

**Auto mode is on in this session right now.** It sits between "approve everything yourself" and "approve nothing." Instead of a fixed allowlist, it judges each action in context, so the same command can be fine in one task and flagged in another. It's not a guarantee, so for sensitive repos or production credentials, default mode is safer.

### Other settings people sometimes call "modes"
- **Fast mode** (`/fast`): faster output from the same Opus model. It's about speed, not permissions.
- **Allow/deny rules**: in `settings.json` (or via `/permissions`) you can always allow or always block specific tools or commands, like `npm test`, in any mode.
- **Effort level**: controls how much I think before answering. Lower is faster, higher is more thorough.

A common pattern is to start a big feature in plan mode, agree on the plan, then switch to accept edits or auto mode to carry it out.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
## Is Docker worth it just for skip-permissions?

**Probably not for you right now.** Here's why:

- **Auto mode already gives you most of the benefit.** You get far fewer prompts, and the risky actions still get caught.
- **The setup isn't free.** You'd install Docker or OrbStack, write a devcontainer config, sort out file mounts, and reinstall your tools inside the container. Things also get a bit slower and clunkier, especially file watching and GUI tools.
- **Bypass mostly pays off for long unattended runs.** That means kicking off a task and walking away for an hour, or running several agents at once. If you're at the keyboard watching anyway, the gain is small.

It becomes worth it if you start doing those long or parallel autonomous runs often. Even then, Claude Code on the web covers a lot of the same need without local setup.

## Using claude.ai/code

It runs Claude Code in a VM that Anthropic manages. How it works:

1. **Put your code on GitHub.** Web sessions clone from a GitHub repo. **This folder isn't a git repo yet**, so you'd need to `git init` and push it to GitHub first. Make the repo private if it's a take-home.
2. Go to **claude.ai/code** and install the **Claude GitHub app** on that repo.
3. **Set up an environment.** You choose how much network access the VM gets and add any environment variables. You can also add a setup script, e.g. `pip install -r requirements.txt`.
4. **Give it a task.** It works on its own in the VM and pushes to a branch, and you can open a PR from there. You can watch it, steer it while it runs, or close the tab and come back later.
5. **Pull it back to your laptop if you want.** Sessions can be moved into your local CLI ("teleport") so you can keep going locally.

## Connecting your API key

This depends on what the key is for, because there are two separate things here.

**1. Paying for Claude Code itself.** This isn't done with an API key. Web sessions run on your **claude.ai subscription** (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise). I don't believe you can plug a Console API key in to pay for usage there. If you've only been using Claude Code through an API key and don't have a subscription, you'd need one.

**2. Your project's code calling the Anthropic API.** For example, if the take-home makes requests to Claude, add the key as an environment variable, like `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...`, in the environment settings from step 3. Your code can then read it when it runs in the VM. Two cautions:
- Anything in that session, including Claude, can read the key. Consider making a separate key with a spending limit in the Anthropic Console.
- Never commit the key to the repo. Keep it in a `.env` file listed in `.gitignore` locally, and in the environment settings on the web.

The web product changes fast, so check the exact billing and environment-variable details in the Claude Code docs. I can look them up for you, or set this folder up as a git repo with a proper `.gitignore` so it's ready to push.

I checked both questions against the current Claude Code docs.

## 1. Getting transcripts out of a cloud session

There's no download or export button for cloud sessions. Your options:

- **Teleport it to your laptop:** run `claude --teleport` (or `/teleport` inside the CLI). It checks out the session's branch and loads the full conversation into your terminal. You then have your own local copy, and new work there doesn't sync back to the cloud.
  - **Requirements:** a clean git state, a checkout of the same repo, the branch pushed to GitHub, and being logged in with your claude.ai account (not an API key).
- **Save it as text:** once it's loaded locally, `/export` saves a readable plain-text transcript.
- **Raw local files:** local sessions are saved as JSONL in `~/.claude/projects/<project-path>/<session-id>.jsonl` and kept for 30 days by default. The docs don't say whether teleporting writes one of these files, so I wouldn't rely on that.
- **Share a link:** the web UI can share a session by link, with visibility set to Private or Public on Pro/Max. That lets someone view it but doesn't give you a file.

## 2. Moving a local session to the cloud

**The CLI can't move a running session to the cloud.** The docs say directly that you can pull cloud sessions down but can't push a terminal session up. What exists instead:

- **`claude --cloud "task"`** starts a *new* cloud session for the current repo. Your local conversation doesn't come with it.
  - The VM clones from GitHub, so push your commits first.
  - With no GitHub remote, the CLI uploads a bundle of the repo instead. That bundle includes uncommitted changes to tracked files, but not new files you haven't added to git. `.env` and key files are left out.
- **`claude -p "message" --cloud <session-id>`** sends a follow-up message to a cloud session that's already running.
- **The Claude Desktop app** can send a local session to the cloud from its **Open in** menu. That's the only documented way to move an existing session.

**Docs' suggested way to carry context over:** plan locally, save the plan to a file in the repo, commit and push it, then run `claude --cloud "Execute the plan in docs/plan.md"`. Anything from your local conversation the cloud session needs has to go in the prompt or in a committed file.

This folder isn't a git repo yet, and every cloud path needs one: teleport needs the branch pushed to GitHub, and `--cloud` needs at least one commit even without GitHub. If you want, I can run `git init` here, add a `.gitignore` that covers `.env`, and make the first commit.

Sources: [code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web), [code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions)
